title: Epidemiological foundations
objective: Define the population, outcome, denominator and time period before choosing an analysis.
summary: Define the population, selection process, outcome and time horizon first. Prevalence counts existing cases in a population at a specified time or period. Incidence concerns new cases: cumulative risk concerns initially disease-free people over a fixed period, whereas an incidence rate uses their time at risk. Changing diagnosis counts can reflect population size, testing or case definitions, not just disease occurrence. Study design and ascertainment determine what comparisons mean.
challenge: A clinic sees twice as many new diagnoses this year. Which population, testing and time-period information would you need before concluding that disease risk has doubled?
steps: This fictional one-year cohort starts with 300 disease-free exposed and 300 disease-free unexposed people, with complete follow-up and comparable case ascertainment. There are 30 and 15 first cases respectively. The risk form takes four cell counts, not group totals: columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent. Enter top row 30, 15 and bottom row 270, 285. Then one-year risks are 10% and 5%, RR = 2 and exposed-minus-unexposed risk difference = 5 percentage points. These are observational associations; they do not by themselves establish an exposure effect.
r:
# Fictional cohort: initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up,
# comparable case ascertainment; events are first cases in distinct people.
events <- c(30,15); at_risk <- c(300,300)
print(data.frame(Group=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),Events=events,At_risk=at_risk,Risk=events/at_risk))
print(c(risk_ratio=(30/300)/(15/300),risk_difference=30/300-15/300))
barplot(events/at_risk,names.arg=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylim=c(0,0.15),ylab="One-year risk",main="Observed association, not a causal estimate")
# If follow-up durations differ, examine person-time and censoring; do not label these risks incidence rates.

title: From association to causal questions
objective: Recognise confounding and define the assumptions behind a causal comparison.
summary: A causal question compares well-defined alternatives in the same target population. Baseline age can influence exposure and outcome, making the exposed groups incomparable. Adjustment needs a justified causal structure and assumptions, not just a change in an estimate. Conditioning on a mediator can remove part of a total effect and does not automatically identify a direct effect; conditioning on a common consequence can induce selection bias.
challenge: Age can affect both treatment choice and outcome. Why might adjusting for age help, while adjusting for a consequence of treatment change the effect we are trying to estimate?
steps: Assume initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up and age measured before exposure. Constructed counts are 44/200 exposed versus 26/200 unexposed. For the crude risk grid, columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent: enter top row 44, 26 and bottom row 156, 174. Younger risks are 4/40 and 16/160; older risks are 40/160 and 10/40. Crude RR is about 1.69, but each within-age RR is 1. Standardising both groups to a 50% younger, 50% older population gives risk 17.5% in each. This illustrates age imbalance; neither equality after adjustment nor a crude association proves a causal conclusion.
r:
# Constructed baseline-age example: initially disease-free people,
# first cases over one year with complete follow-up. Age precedes exposure.
data <- data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),Exposed_events=c(4,40),Exposed_total=c(40,160),Unexposed_events=c(16,10),Unexposed_total=c(160,40))
data$Exposed_risk <- data$Exposed_events/data$Exposed_total
data$Unexposed_risk <- data$Unexposed_events/data$Unexposed_total
print(data)
print(c(crude_RR=(44/200)/(26/200)))
print(data.frame(Age=data$Age,Within_age_RR=data$Exposed_risk/data$Unexposed_risk))
# Apply the SAME target-population weights to both groups.
weights <- c(0.5,0.5)
standardised <- c(Exposed=sum(weights*data$Exposed_risk),Unexposed=sum(weights*data$Unexposed_risk))
print(standardised)
print(c(standardised_RR=unname(standardised[1]/standardised[2])))
barplot(rbind(data$Exposed_risk,data$Unexposed_risk),beside=TRUE,names.arg=data$Age,legend.text=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylab="Observed risk",main="Same within-age risks; different age mix")
# Within-stratum agreement is not proof that every source of bias has been removed.

title: Comparing paired measurements
objective: Recognise pairing, analyse differences and interpret a confidence interval.
summary: Pairing means repeated measurements on the same people or explicitly matched units. A paired t test analyses within-pair differences, with independence between pairs. For exact small-sample inference the differences are normally distributed; inspect their distribution and unusual values. Two sets of patients attending the same clinic at different times are not automatically paired, and different patients may still be clustered.
challenge: The example has a before and an after measurement on each of the same eight people. Why is a paired analysis appropriate, and what design questions would you ask if the two periods instead contained different, unmatched people?
steps: Use Try in StatsDirect to open the paired t test with Before and After. The worksheet contains eight fictional, independently sampled participants. The comparison is Before minus After, so a positive difference means a fall. Use a 95% confidence level to compare with the R example. Inspect the differences and interpret the estimated mean difference and interval before the P value; an uncontrolled before–after change alone does not establish causation.
r:
# Fictional paired measurements: same eight people, same row order.
before <- c(142,136,151,145,139,148,132,155)
after <- c(135,134,143,141,136,140,130,147)
data <- data.frame(Before=before, After=after)
print(data)
# StatsDirect uses first minus second for this selection.
# Assume independent people; small-sample t inference models normal differences.
change <- before - after
print(t.test(before, after, paired=TRUE, conf.level=0.95))
plot(before, after, pch=19, xlab="Before", ylab="After", main="Fictional paired measurements")
abline(0,1,lty=2)
# The diagonal shows equal before/after values; this is not an agreement analysis.
# Try: inspect change, change one after value, rerun, and explain the interval.
# A change without a suitable control comparison does not establish causation.
previousChallenges: If the average measurement falls after an intervention, what else would you need before claiming the intervention caused the change?

The same eight people have a measurement taken before and after an intervention, with each person's two values on the same row. Why are these paired observations? How would the analysis change if different people were measured in the two periods?

title: Variation, precision and uncertainty
objective: Separate standard deviation from standard error and confidence intervals.
summary: Standard deviation describes variation between observations. Standard error describes sampling variation of an estimator. For independent observations from the same population, the mean has SE = population SD / sqrt(n), estimated using the sample SD. A nominal 95% confidence procedure targets 95% repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions. These 12 waits are skewed: a small-sample t interval is an illustration to scrutinise, not an assurance of reliable coverage.
challenge: For independent observations from the same population with a fixed, finite variance, why does quadrupling sample size halve the theoretical standard error of the mean? Why might the sample SD and estimated SE still vary between samples?
steps: Open the descriptive summary for the fictional waiting times. Compare mean, median, SD and the 95% confidence interval. Inspect the long wait and the distribution before interpreting the small-sample t interval. Do not delete an observation merely because it is large. The appropriate summary depends on whether the question concerns an average, a typical wait or the long-wait tail.
r:
# Fictional clinic waits; no patient data.
wait <- c(12,15,14,18,21,16,19,13,45,17,20,22)
print(data.frame(Waiting_minutes=wait))
print(c(mean=mean(wait), median=median(wait), SD=sd(wait), SE=sd(wait)/sqrt(length(wait))))
# An illustrative normal-theory mean CI: only 12 skewed observations.
# Exact t coverage assumes independent normal observations; that is questionable here.
# A non-significant normality test would not establish the assumption.
mean_ci <- t.test(wait, conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("Illustrative 95% t interval for the mean; check assumptions:\n")
print(mean_ci)
hist(wait, breaks=8, main="Fictional clinic waiting times", xlab="Minutes")
# Try: explain why mean and median differ; inspect the outlier without silently deleting it.
previousChallenges: Why would collecting four times as many independent observations halve the standard error but not necessarily change the standard deviation?

title: Interpreting a diagnostic test
objective: Choose the right denominator for sensitivity, specificity and predictive value.
summary: Sensitivity is the proportion positive among people with the condition; specificity is the proportion negative among those without it. Predictive values condition on the test result instead. The fictional sample represents a population with 10% prevalence and a reliable reference diagnosis. Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity also need to be applicable to the intended case mix, threshold and reference standard.
challenge: If the condition becomes rarer while sensitivity and specificity stay the same, what happens to the proportion of positive results that are false positives?
steps: In the diagnostic grid, columns represent disease present/absent and rows test positive/negative: enter top row 72, 81 and bottom row 18, 729. These are true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives respectively. These fictional independent observations give sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%, PPV about 47.1% and NPV about 97.6%. The R example labels a 95% exact binomial interval for sensitivity; different interval methods need not match numerically.
r:
# Fictional diagnostic study. Rows: test result; columns: disease status.
tp <- 72; fn <- 18; fp <- 81; tn <- 729
counts <- matrix(c(tp,fp,fn,tn),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=list(Test=c("Positive","Negative"),Disease=c("Present","Absent")))
print(counts)
print(c(sensitivity=tp/(tp+fn), specificity=tn/(tn+fp), PPV=tp/(tp+fp), NPV=tn/(tn+fn)))
# Treat diagnoses as reliable and observations as independent.
# This is a sensitivity interval, not an interval for all four measures.
sensitivity_ci <- binom.test(tp,tp+fn,conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("95% exact binomial CI for sensitivity (may be conservative):\n")
print(sensitivity_ci)
barplot(counts, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE, main="Fictional diagnostic counts", ylab="People")

title: Absolute and relative benefit
objective: Interpret absolute risk reduction, relative risk and the follow-up period.
summary: Over one year, 28/200 controls and 16/200 programme participants have at least one unplanned admission. The estimated absolute risk reduction (control minus programme) is 6 percentage points; programme-to-control RR is about 0.57 and NNT for benefit rounds up to 17. These are uncertain point estimates. The illustrated risk-difference interval includes zero and possible harm, so it does not establish benefit.
challenge: Would the same relative risk imply the same absolute benefit in a population with a much lower baseline risk?
steps: Assume individual randomisation, independent participants and complete one-year follow-up. In the NNT form enter 16 people with at least one admission among 200 programme participants and 28 among 200 controls. Count people, not repeated admissions. Interpret NNT 17 as the point estimate for preventing one additional person having an admission over one year. A risk-difference interval spanning zero gives NNT uncertainty extending through infinity into both benefit and harm; do not present a single ordinary finite NNT interval.
r:
# Fictional individually randomised programme; complete one-year follow-up.
# Events count people with at least one unplanned admission, not repeated admissions.
events <- c(16,28); totals <- c(200,200)
risk <- events/totals
print(data.frame(Group=c("Programme","Usual care"),Events=events,Total=totals,Risk=risk))
arr <- risk[2]-risk[1]
print(c(absolute_reduction=arr,relative_risk=risk[1]/risk[2],NNT=ceiling(1/arr)))
# Keep the CI direction consistent with arr: usual care minus programme.
# Base R uses its own interval method, which can differ from StatsDirect.
comparison <- prop.test(rev(events),rev(totals),correct=FALSE,conf.level=0.95)
arr_ci <- comparison$conf.int
cat("95% CI for risk reduction, usual care minus programme:\n")
print(arr_ci)
print(comparison)
# This interval includes zero: benefit is not established and some harm is compatible.
# Inverting an interval across zero requires separate benefit/harm branches via infinity.
# Do not report its reciprocals as one ordinary finite NNT interval.
barplot(risk,names.arg=c("Programme","Usual care"),ylim=c(0,0.2),ylab="One-year event risk")

learningObjectives: Report absolute and relative effects with the same outcome and time horizon.
Keep subtraction direction consistent across estimates and intervals.

keyConcepts.explanation: For this adverse outcome, control risk minus programme risk is the absolute risk reduction. Six percentage points is a difference of 0.06, not a 6% relative reduction.
An identical relative risk can imply different absolute differences in populations with different baseline risks, provided the relative effect is applicable.
NNT is a reciprocal of an absolute risk difference at a stated time horizon. If the difference interval crosses zero, its reciprocal has separate benefit and harm branches through infinity.

misconceptions.claim: An NNT point estimate of 17 establishes benefit.
misconceptions.correction: The interval for the underlying risk difference includes no effect and possible harm.

misconceptions.claim: NNT counts admissions prevented, including repeated admissions in the same person.
misconceptions.correction: This example counts people with at least one admission. Recurrent-event questions require a different analysis.

workedExample.interpretation: Programme risk is 8% versus 14% in controls: ARR 6 percentage points, RR 4/7 and NNT point estimate 17. Assess uncertainty, harms and practical importance together.

title: Association is not causation
objective: Interpret a regression slope without confusing prediction with causation.
summary: Each row is a different fictional service, with appointment duration and a mean satisfaction score on a 0–100 scale. The line describes a service-level association; it does not establish an individual-level or causal effect. Conventional small-sample regression inference assumes a linear conditional mean, independent errors with constant variance and normal errors. Inspect residuals and study design; the predictor need not be normally distributed.
challenge: A service with longer appointment slots has higher satisfaction. What alternative explanations could produce this association?
steps: Use Satisfaction as the dependent variable and Appointment minutes as the predictor in simple linear regression. The eight services are treated as independent for this illustration. Inspect the scatterplot and residuals; consider service case mix and measurement. The R intervals are 95% intervals for model coefficients, not prediction intervals for a future service. Do not extrapolate beyond 10–24 minutes without justification.
r:
# Eight fictional services: each row is a separate service, not a patient.
# Satisfaction is the service mean on a 0-100 scale.
# For conventional small-sample inference assume linear mean, independent,
# constant-variance normal errors. Predictor normality is not required.
data <- data.frame(Satisfaction=c(58,61,60,67,65,73,71,78),Minutes=c(10,12,14,16,18,20,22,24))
print(data)
fit <- lm(Satisfaction ~ Minutes, data=data)
print(summary(fit))
cat("95% confidence intervals for regression coefficients (not predictions):\n")
print(confint(fit,level=0.95))
plot(data$Minutes,data$Satisfaction,pch=19,xlab="Appointment minutes",ylab="Satisfaction",main="Association in fictional service data")
abline(fit)
plot(fitted(fit),residuals(fit),pch=19,xlab="Fitted satisfaction",ylab="Residual",main="Check the model, not just the slope")
abline(h=0,lty=2)
# Explain a potential service-level confounder; do not infer individual causation.

learningObjectives: Interpret a slope at the level of the observed units.

keyConcepts.explanation: A relationship between service means is a service-level association. It need not describe the relationship between individual patients.
Exact conventional small-sample t inference assumes normal independent errors with constant variance around the specified linear mean. Predictors themselves need not be normally distributed.
A confidence interval for a mean response differs from a prediction interval for a new observation. Extrapolation adds assumptions not checked by a good fit within the observed range.

misconceptions.claim: A statistically significant slope proves longer appointments cause satisfaction.
misconceptions.correction: Service case mix, staffing and other factors can explain association.

misconceptions.claim: A high R-squared demonstrates accurate predictions for a new hospital.
misconceptions.correction: Performance in new data requires validation and assessment of calibration and prediction error.

teachingPrompts.prompt: What extra uncertainty belongs in a prediction interval for a new service?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: It includes residual variation of a new outcome as well as uncertainty about the fitted mean, under the model assumptions.

title: Comparing population rates
objective: Explain a crude rate difference using age-specific rates and a common standard population.
summary: A rate divides events by time at risk. Different age structures can produce different crude rates even when age-specific rates are identical. Direct standardisation applies the same reference weights to each population. A standardised rate is a comparison measure; report its reference population, uncertainty and age-specific pattern.
challenge: Two areas have identical younger and older age-specific rates but different crude rates. How could this happen, and what would a fair age-standardised comparison require?
steps: The worksheet has two rows: younger, then older. For Area A select Events (40, 800), Person-years (20000, 80000), then Reference population (75000, 25000) in Direct standardization. Use default row labels and multiplier 100000. The crude rate is 840 per 100000 person-years; the directly standardised rate is 400. Area B has 160 and 200 events in 80000 and 20000 person-years: its crude rate is 360 but the same standardised rate is 400. R displays both areas. Compare point estimates with matching units; StatsDirect also supplies intervals.
r:
# Fictional independent event counts; rows are younger, older.
# Person-time is time actually at risk, not the number of people enrolled.
area_a <- data.frame(Events=c(40,800),Person_years=c(20000,80000))
area_b <- data.frame(Events=c(160,200),Person_years=c(80000,20000))
reference <- c(75000,25000); weights <- reference/sum(reference)
rate_a <- area_a$Events/area_a$Person_years
rate_b <- area_b$Events/area_b$Person_years
crude <- c(A=sum(area_a$Events)/sum(area_a$Person_years),B=sum(area_b$Events)/sum(area_b$Person_years))*100000
standardised <- c(A=sum(weights*rate_a),B=sum(weights*rate_b))*100000
print(data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),A_per_100000=rate_a*100000,B_per_100000=rate_b*100000,Weight=weights))
print(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised))
barplot(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised),beside=TRUE,legend.text=TRUE,ylab="Events per 100000 person-years",main="Fictional areas, common age-specific rates")
# Point-estimate illustration. Do not give this weighted rate the CI for a single crude count.
# Equal standardised rates do not prove equality or remove all sources of bias.

title: Appraising a trial result
objective: Explain what a numerical trial result can and cannot establish.
summary: Read the research question, allocation, follow-up and outcome measurement before the P value. Risk of bias concerns a particular result; reporting completeness and a large sample do not guarantee validity. Missing outcomes can break the comparability intended by randomisation. Explain effect size, uncertainty and applicability separately.
challenge: A randomised trial reports outcomes for 80 of 100 programme participants and all 100 controls. Before accepting its claim of benefit, what would you ask about the 20 missing outcomes?
steps: Fictional one-year adverse outcomes are observed in 20/80 programme participants and 30/100 controls. Try in StatsDirect opens the risk comparison: columns programme/control, top row events 20, 30; bottom row observed non-events 60, 70. The observed-data RR is 5/6. This omits 20 programme participants. R shows how their unknown outcomes permit full-group programme risks from 20% to 40%, against 30% in controls. These bounds describe missing-outcome uncertainty, not a 95% confidence interval.
r:
# Fictional individually randomised trial, one-year binary adverse outcome.
randomised <- c(Programme=100,Control=100)
observed <- c(Programme=80,Control=100)
events <- c(Programme=20,Control=30)
missing <- randomised-observed
print(data.frame(Randomised=randomised,Observed=observed,Events=events,Missing=missing))
observed_rr <- (events[1]/observed[1])/(events[2]/observed[2]); print(observed_rr)
programme_bounds <- c(Lower=20/100,Upper=(20+20)/100)
control_risk <- 30/100
arr_bounds <- c(Lower=control_risk-programme_bounds[2],Upper=control_risk-programme_bounds[1])
print(programme_bounds); print(arr_bounds)
plot(c(1,1),programme_bounds,type="b",pch=19,xlim=c(0.5,1.5),ylim=c(0,0.5),xaxt="n",xlab="Programme: possible one-year risk",ylab="Risk",main="Missing-outcome bounds, not a confidence interval")
abline(h=control_risk,lty=2)
legend("topleft", "Control risk: 30%", lty=2, bty="n")
# Bounds assume all 20 unknown outcomes are either non-events or events.
# They do not include sampling uncertainty or assert that either extreme is plausible.

title: Understanding missing data
objective: Describe missingness and avoid treating a filled-in value as observed information.
summary: Document the amount, pattern and reasons for missingness before choosing an analysis. MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe assumptions about the missingness process. MAR allows dependence on observed information; it is not a synonym for a random-looking pattern. Replacing missing values with a mean does not restore information or valid uncertainty.
challenge: Six of eight people return a symptom score. How might the interpretation change if the two missing people felt much worse, rather than simply forgetting an appointment?
steps: Scores range from 0 to 40, with higher scores worse. The StatsDirect worksheet contains only the six observed scores: 20, 22, 18, 26, 24, 30. Its mean is 23.33 for responders, not necessarily all eight people. R retains two explicit NA positions and shows full-group mean bounds of 17.5 to 27.5 if each missing score can lie anywhere from 0 to 40. This is an illustration of assumptions, not a confidence interval or a recommended imputation method.
r:
# Fictional scores, allowable range 0–40; higher is worse.
score <- c(20,22,18,26,24,30,NA,NA)
print(data.frame(Person=seq_along(score),Score=score,Missing=is.na(score)))
observed_mean <- mean(score,na.rm=TRUE)
mean_bounds <- (sum(score,na.rm=TRUE)+sum(is.na(score))*c(0,40))/length(score)
print(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Missing=sum(is.na(score))))
print(mean_bounds)
filled <- replace(score,is.na(score),observed_mean)
print(c(Observed_SD=sd(score,na.rm=TRUE),Mean_filled_SD=sd(filled)))
barplot(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Lower_bound=mean_bounds[1],Upper_bound=mean_bounds[2]),ylim=c(0,40),ylab="Symptom score",main="Missing values: bounds are not confidence limits")
# Mean filling is shown as a pitfall: it understates uncertainty if treated as real data.
# No method can identify the missing outcomes from these observed values alone.

learningObjectives: Distinguish MCAR, MAR and MNAR assumptions.
Explain why complete-case analysis and single imputation need justification.

keyConcepts.explanation: MCAR means missingness does not depend on observed or unobserved values. Under MAR, after conditioning on observed information it does not additionally depend on the missing values. Under MNAR that dependence remains.

Complete-case validity depends on the estimand, model and missingness process; MCAR is sufficient in many simple settings but is not always necessary. Multiple imputation needs a suitable model and appropriate pooling of uncertainty.
Observed data alone cannot generally distinguish MAR from MNAR. Use reasons for absence, auxiliary measurements and scientifically defensible sensitivity scenarios.

misconceptions.claim: MAR can be proved from an observed-data test.

misconceptions.claim: Mean imputation increases sample size with no downside.

title: Checking prediction performance
objective: Assess predictions against outcomes not used to develop the model.
summary: A model can rank outcomes well yet predict systematically wrong values. Evaluate calibration and prediction error as well as association. Performance on the development data is usually optimistic. Internal validation must repeat the modelling process; evaluation in a new relevant setting addresses transportability. A tiny illustration cannot establish clinical usefulness.
challenge: If we add ten points to every predicted score, can its correlation with observed scores stay unchanged while its prediction error gets worse?
steps: The fictional predictions were fixed before these eight outcomes were observed. Select Observed score as outcome and Predicted score as predictor in simple regression to inspect calibration; a descriptive calibration line is not a newly validated prediction model. R compares the original predictions with the same predictions shifted upward by ten. Correlation is unchanged; RMSE rises from about 1.58 to 10.12 points. Compare with the identity line, not just the fitted slope.
r:
# Fictional independent evaluation sample. Predictions were fixed in advance.
predicted <- seq(10,80,by=10)
observed <- c(12,18,31,39,51,59,72,78)
shifted <- predicted+10
rmse <- function(p) sqrt(mean((observed-p)^2))
print(data.frame(Observed=observed,Predicted=predicted,Shifted=shifted))
metrics <- rbind(Original=c(Correlation=cor(observed,predicted),RMSE=rmse(predicted),Mean_error=mean(predicted-observed)),Shifted=c(Correlation=cor(observed,shifted),RMSE=rmse(shifted),Mean_error=mean(shifted-observed)))
print(metrics)
calibration <- lm(observed~predicted); print(coef(calibration))
plot(predicted,observed,pch=19,xlim=c(0,100),ylim=c(0,100),xlab="Predicted score",ylab="Observed score",main="Correlation does not establish calibration")
points(shifted,observed,pch=1,col="blue"); abline(0,1,lty=2)
legend("topleft",c("Original","Shifted +10","Ideal agreement"),pch=c(19,1,NA),lty=c(NA,NA,2),col=c("black","blue","black"))
# This eight-person example demonstrates metrics; it does not validate clinical use.
# Do not retune the model on these outcomes and then call the same data an untouched test set.

title: Combining study results
objective: Explain inverse-variance weighting and decide whether a pooled effect answers a coherent question.
summary: Pooling requires comparable populations, contrasts, outcomes and follow-up, together with an assessment of bias and dependence. Inverse-variance weights favour more precise estimates. A fixed-effect illustration assumes a common underlying effect. Random-effects models allow between-study variation but cannot repair biased studies or justify combining incompatible questions.
challenge: Three studies estimate the same risk difference, but one has twice the standard error of the others. Should it receive twice the weight, half the weight or a quarter of the weight?
steps: The fictional independent studies report one-year adverse-outcome risk differences (programme minus control) of −0.04, −0.08 and −0.03, with SEs 0.02, 0.04 and 0.02. In Summary meta-analysis choose Risk Difference, then Standard Error, and select the two named columns; use default study labels and 95% confidence. Compare the fixed-effect estimate with R: −0.04, 95% normal interval about −0.0661 to −0.0139. This exercise assumes approximately normal estimates and a common underlying effect; it is not a complete systematic review.
r:
# Three fictional independent trials: same adverse outcome and one-year horizon.
# Risk difference = programme minus control. SE, not SD, is supplied.
effect <- c(-0.04,-0.08,-0.03); se <- c(0.02,0.04,0.02)
weight <- 1/se^2
pooled <- sum(weight*effect)/sum(weight)
pooled_se <- sqrt(1/sum(weight))
pooled_ci <- pooled+c(-1,1)*qnorm(0.975)*pooled_se
q <- sum(weight*(effect-pooled)^2)
print(data.frame(Study=1:3,Risk_difference=effect,SE=se,Percent_weight=100*weight/sum(weight)))
print(c(Pooled=pooled,SE=pooled_se,Lower=pooled_ci[1],Upper=pooled_ci[2],Q=q))
lower <- effect-qnorm(0.975)*se; upper <- effect+qnorm(0.975)*se
plot(effect,1:3,pch=19,xlim=range(c(lower,upper,0)),ylim=c(0,3.5),yaxt="n",xlab="Risk difference: programme minus control",ylab="",main="Fictional fixed-effect illustration")
segments(lower,1:3,upper,1:3); abline(v=0,lty=2)
points(pooled,0,pch=18); segments(pooled_ci[1],0,pooled_ci[2],0)
axis(2,at=0:3,labels=c("Pooled","Study 1","Study 2","Study 3"),las=1)
# The interval estimates a common effect under the model; not a prediction interval.
# Few studies give weak information about heterogeneity and publication bias.

learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret inverse-variance weights.

keyConcepts.explanation: For independent approximately normal estimates with known or adequately estimated SEs, fixed-effect weights are 1/SE². Doubling SE gives one quarter of the weight.

Overlapping participants, selective reporting and unpublished results can undermine a synthesis. Choose eligible comparisons before looking at their P values.

practiceQuestions.objective: Explain inverse-variance weighting and decide whether a pooled effect answers a coherent question.
practiceQuestions.stem: In a fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis, Study A has SE 0.02 and Study B has SE 0.04 for estimates on the same scale. What is the ratio of A’s weight to B’s weight?

options.feedback: That reverses the inverse-variance weighting.
The smaller SE receives more, not less, weight.
Equal weighting ignores their different precisions.
Weights use squared SE, not SE itself.

practiceQuestions.hint: Variance is the square of the standard error; then take its reciprocal.
practiceQuestions.lesson: Pooling requires comparable populations, contrasts, outcomes and follow-up, together with an assessment of bias and dependence. Inverse-variance weights favour more precise estimates. A fixed-effect illustration assumes a common underlying effect. Random-effects models allow between-study variation but cannot repair biased studies or justify combining incompatible questions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The weights are 2500 and 625, so A receives four times B’s weight. This does not make A four times as free from bias; inverse-variance weighting represents statistical precision under the model.
